parole.testo: From Low German blick, from Middle Low German bleck, from Old Saxon *blek, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką. Compare Danish blik (< Middle Low German bleck), German Blech (< Old High German bleh).
From Low German bolt, from Middle Low German bolte, from Old Saxon bolt, from Proto-West Germanic *bolt.

Borrowed from Low German cauwe, from Middle Low German kâ, from Old Saxon *kaha, from Proto-West Germanic *kahu, from Proto-Germanic *kawō (“jackdaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewH-. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kaie.

parole.significato: to a no longer attached or stuck state (no longer stuck to something, generally); loose, off, untied
parole.testo: From Low German los (“free, loose”), from Middle Low German lōs, from Old Saxon lōs, from Proto-West Germanic *laus. See also Danish los and Norwegian loss, Dutch loos. Doublet of lös.

From Low German leschen (“to extinguish”), from Middle Low German leschen, from Old Saxon leskan, from Proto-West Germanic *leskan. Related to modern Dutch lessen and modern German löschen. According to Svenska Akademiens ordbok the original meaning has been "to make something lay down" and related

From Low German nück, nücke, from Middle Low German *nuken, from Old Saxon *hnukian, from Proto-West Germanic *hnukēn, ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *hnukāną (“to curve, be bent”). Compare Dutch nuk.

parole.significato: to have the eyes turned in different directions, either deliberately (and temporarily) or due to strabismus
parole.testo: From Low German schelen, from Middle Low German schēle, from Old Saxon *skelh, from Proto-West Germanic *skelh (“squinting, crooked”).
From Low German schinke, from Middle Low German schinke, from Old Saxon skinka, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō. Cognate with English skink and Icelandic skinka.

parole.significato: a chimney (vertical tube or hollow column; a flue)
parole.testo: From Low German Schornstein, compound of schore (“support”) (ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skeran (“to cut”)) and Stein (“rock”) (from Middle Low German sten). Compare Danish skorsten and Norwegian Nynorsk skorstein.
From Low German slagge, slakke, from Middle Low German slagge, perhaps from slagen (“to strike”), from Old Saxon slegi, from Proto-West Germanic *slagi.
Borrowed from Low German smuggeln, from Middle Low German smugen, from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to slip through, creep”). Doublet of smyga.
Related to snut (“mouth”), also "snout," probably borrowed through Low German and ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *snūt.

From Low German stickelber (“gooseberry”), the first element from Low German stickel (“tip, stinger”) (ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *stekan) and the second adapted to match Swedish bär (“berry”).

parole.significato: weight (what something weighs, measured in for example kilograms)
parole.testo: From Low German and Middle Low German wicht, from Old Saxon wiht, from Proto-West Germanic *wihti.
